newsitem.title: USA: Clinton lauds Fujimori on Lima hostage crisis.
newsitem.headline: Clinton lauds Fujimori on Lima hostage crisis.

text.p: Peru's President Alberto Fujimori on Monday discussed his handling of the Lima hostage crisis with U.S. President Bill Clinton, who praised him for blending firmness with humanitarian concern.

"The president told President Fujimori that he was skilfully walking a very fine line ... between resolving this crisis peacefully without giving in to terror," White House spokesman David Johnson said after the 20-minute meeting.

Fujimori stopped off in Washington following an emergency summit with Japanese Prime Minister Ryutaro Hashimoto in Toronto on Saturday. The Lima hostages have been held in the Japanese embassy since Dec. 17 by Marxist guerrillas.
Before the White House meeting, Fujimori dismissed suggestions of any "peace accord" with the hostage-takers.

"Peru has paid too high a cost to impose law and order ... to throw it all overboard and give in to the extortion of a gaggle of human rights violators," Fujimori, speaking in Spanish, told the Organisation of American States.

He referred to Tupac Amaru Revolutionary Movement (MRTA) rebels who hold 72 hostages in Peru and demand the release of jailed comrades, improved prison conditions, an overhaul of Peru's secret court system for people accused of terrorism and an end to Fujimori's free-market economic reforms.
At a news conference later, Fujimori said release of MRTA prisoners was "out of the question" and defended Peru's prisons as being vastly improved over the last four years.
He said there was a framework in place for preliminary talks with the rebels, but that while there was a "big range of talks" there was "a very narrow range of concessions."

Fujimori said he had discussed with Canadian officials a plan for possible asylum for MRTA rebels in a foreign country, but did not say which, and asked rhetorically, "I wonder if there are other countries willing to accept these terrorists?"

Asked about Lori Berenson, a freelance journalist from New York sentenced to life in prison by a Peruvian military court for involvement with MRTA, Fujimori said she was in "good condition, good health." He did not address requests by Berenson for a new civilian trial.

U.S. Assistant Secretary of State Jeff Davidow discussed U.S. concerns about the Berenson case with Fujimori on Saturday, notably about her military trial and the conditions of her detention, the State Department said.

Fujimori also said he had been in contact with the U.S. anti-drug czar, retired Army Gen. Barry McCaffrey, and said Washington would cooperate with Peru in working to stop drug trafficking on Peruvian rivers.

At their emergency summit on Saturday, Fujimori and Hashimoto agreed to push for direct talks with the rebels but ruled out conceding to the guerrillas' demand for the liberation of about 400 MRTA members jailed in Peru.

The leader of the MRTA, who is one of about 15 heavily-armed guerrillas occupying the mansion in an upscale Lima neighbourhood, reiterated on Sunday that any government move to force them out would end in tragedy.

"We know (an assault by the Peruvian army) would be tragic for the gentlemen held captive here. We are sorry for them and for their families," Nestor Cerpa Cartolino said in an interview with two Spanish newspapers.
The rebels originally took more than 500 hostages during a cocktail party at the diplomatic mansion.
The remaining 72 captives in the mined and booby-trapped residence include two Peruvian ministers, the Japanese and Bolivian ambassadors, about two dozen Japanese businessmen and Fujimori's brother.
